Chapter 2: The Mindset of Control—What Drives Abusive Partners.
Behind every controlling relationship, there’s a particular way of thinking—a mindset you might not see on the surface, but one that shapes every interaction.
These beliefs don’t always get spoken out loud. But they’re there, guiding actions, words, and even the long silences that hang in the air after a heated argument.
Picture this: a partner who insists on deciding everything, from what’s on the dinner table to how the bills get paid.
When you question him, he might snap or retreat into a frosty silence, making it painfully clear that disagreement isn’t welcome.
To the outside world, he could seem charming—maybe even generous or self-deprecating. But behind closed doors, the rules change.
Here’s something people often miss: this kind of behavior isn’t just random or a sign of a bad mood.
It comes from a deep sense of entitlement—the belief that his comfort, his needs, and his opinions are more important than anyone else’s.
You’ll see this entitlement in little ways, like brushing off his partner’s feelings, or in bigger ways—using threats, intimidation, or stonewalling to get his way.
Now, a lot of folks believe that abusers lash out because they can’t control their anger, or because they’re carrying emotional scars from the past.
But the truth is usually a lot more unsettling.
Most controlling partners know exactly what they’re doing.
They pick their words carefully, dial things up or down depending on who’s around, and often save their worst behavior for moments when nobody else is watching.
In public, they might seem loving and attentive, making it almost impossible for friends and family to believe what’s really happening at home.
One woman shared how her partner would explode over the smallest things at home, but suddenly become the perfect host whenever friends visited.
She started doubting herself—thinking, “If he can control himself around others, why not with me?”
Over time, she realized the truth: those outbursts weren’t about losing control—they were about enforcing it.
And this mindset? It’s not limited to just one kind of person.
It cuts across age, background, and status.
Some controlling partners are loud and in-your-face. Others are quiet, even subtle, manipulating things behind the scenes.
But what ties them together is this belief: their partner exists to meet their needs, and any pushback is treated like a threat.
If you’re on the receiving end of this, it can feel incredibly confusing.
He might claim he loves you, or that he’s just trying to help, or even accuse you of being too sensitive.
He may blame his actions on stress, alcohol, or even your own behavior.
But beneath all the excuses, there’s a pattern—a refusal to see you as an equal, and a relentless drive to keep control.
Understanding this mindset is so important.
It shifts the focus, doesn’t it?
Instead of blaming yourself or thinking you just need to try harder to fix things, you start to see what’s really going on: a partner who simply isn’t willing to share power or respect your boundaries.
And that realization?
It’s both sobering and empowering.
Because the problem isn’t a lack of effort or understanding on your part.
It’s a refusal to treat another person with basic respect.
